item.title: Muon
item.description:
Muon (Momentum Orthogonalized by Newton-schulz) is an optimizer tailored for 2D weight matrices (linear and dense layers) in neural networks. Where standard SGD operates in Euclidean/Frobenius geometry and Adam normalizes coordinate-wise (inducing an ℓ∞\ell_\inftyℓ∞​-like update), Muon treats weights as linear operators and restricts updates under the spectral norm.

1. The Variational Formulation: Steepest Descent on Spectral Ball

Let a weight matrix be W∈Rdout×dinW \in \mathbb{R}^{d_{\text{out}} \times d_{\text{in}}}W∈Rdout​×din​ and let G=∇WLG = \nabla_W \mathcal{L}G=∇W​L be its objective gradient (or momentum buffer).

We seek an update ΔW\Delta WΔW that maximizes descent in the first-order Taylor expansion while constraining the spectral norm ∥ΔW∥2≤1\Vert{}\Delta W\Vert{}_2 \le 1∥ΔW∥2​≤1 (the maximum operator stretch):

ΔW∗=arg⁡min⁡∥ΔW∥2≤1⟨G,ΔW⟩=arg⁡min⁡∥ΔW∥2≤1Tr⁡(G⊤ΔW) \Delta W^* = \arg\min_{\Vert{}\Delta W\Vert{}_2 \le 1} \langle G, \Delta W \rangle = \arg\min_{\Vert{}\Delta W\Vert{}_2 \le 1} \operatorname{Tr}(G^\top \Delta W) ΔW∗=arg∥ΔW∥2​≤1min​⟨G,ΔW⟩=arg∥ΔW∥2​≤1min​Tr(G⊤ΔW)

Derivation via Singular Value Decomposition (SVD)

Let the singular value decomposition of GGG be:

G=UΣV⊤=∑i=1rσiuivi⊤,σ1≥σ2≥⋯≥σr>0 G = U \Sigma V^\top = \sum_{i=1}^{r} \sigma_i u_i v_i^\top, \quad \sigma_1 \ge \sigma_2 \ge \dots \ge \sigma_r > 0 G=UΣV⊤=i=1∑r​σi​ui​vi⊤​,σ1​≥σ2​≥⋯≥σr​>0

By Von Neumann’s trace inequality and Hölder’s inequality for Schatten norms (since ∥⋅∥2=∥⋅∥S∞\Vert{}\cdot\Vert{}_2 = \Vert{}\cdot\Vert{}_{S_\infty}∥⋅∥2​=∥⋅∥S∞​​ is dual to the nuclear norm ∥⋅∥∗=∥⋅∥S1\Vert{}\cdot\Vert{}_* = \Vert{}\cdot\Vert{}_{S_1}∥⋅∥∗​=∥⋅∥S1​​):

Tr⁡(G⊤ΔW)≥−∑i=1rσi(G)σi(ΔW) \operatorname{Tr}(G^\top \Delta W) \ge -\sum_{i=1}^{r} \sigma_i(G) \sigma_i(\Delta W) Tr(G⊤ΔW)≥−i=1∑r​σi​(G)σi​(ΔW)

Because ∥ΔW∥2≤1\Vert{}\Delta W\Vert{}_2 \le 1∥ΔW∥2​≤1, each singular value σi(ΔW)≤1\sigma_i(\Delta W) \le 1σi​(ΔW)≤1. The lower bound is achieved when all σi(ΔW)=1\sigma_i(\Delta W) = 1σi​(ΔW)=1 aligned along the singular vectors of GGG:

ΔW∗=−UV⊤ \Delta W^* = - U V^\top ΔW∗=−UV⊤

UV⊤U V^\topUV⊤ is the polar factor (orthogonal projection) of GGG. Instead of letting a few large singular values dominate step sizes, Muon flattens all non-zero singular values to 111, allowing updates along all active spectral directions equally.

2. Fast Orthogonalization via Newton–Schulz Iteration

Computing the exact SVD via Golub-Kahan per step is O(min⁡(din,dout)3)O(\min(d_{\text{in}}, d_{\text{out}})^3)O(min(din​,dout​)3), which is prohibitively slow on GPUs. Muon approximates UV⊤UV^\topUV⊤ using a polynomial Newton–Schulz iteration consisting purely of matrix multiplications.

Assume without loss of generality that X∈Rn×mX \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times m}X∈Rn×m is wide (n≤mn \le mn≤m; if tall, transpose first).

  1. Initial Frobenius normalization: X0=G∥G∥F+ϵ X_0 = \frac{G}{\Vert{}G\Vert{}_F + \epsilon} X0​=∥G∥F​+ϵG​ Since ∥G∥F=∑σi2≥σmax⁡(G)\Vert{}G\Vert{}_F = \sqrt{\sum \sigma_i^2} \ge \sigma_{\max}(G)∥G∥F​=∑σi2​​≥σmax​(G), this guarantees that every singular value σi(X0)≤1\sigma_i(X_0) \le 1σi​(X0​)≤1.
  2. Odd polynomial iteration (Quintic form): Xk+1=aXk+b(XkXk⊤)Xk+c(XkXk⊤)2Xk X_{k+1} = a X_k + b (X_k X_k^\top) X_k + c (X_k X_k^\top)^2 X_k Xk+1​=aXk​+b(Xk​Xk⊤​)Xk​+c(Xk​Xk⊤​)2Xk​ Evaluating on singular values, this applies a 1D mapping ϕ(σ)=aσ+bσ3+cσ5\phi(\sigma) = a\sigma + b\sigma^3 + c\sigma^5ϕ(σ)=aσ+bσ3+cσ5 to every singular value while leaving the singular vectors U,VU, VU,V unchanged. With tuned coefficients: a=3.4445,b=−4.7750,c=2.0315 a = 3.4445, \quad b = -4.7750, \quad c = 2.0315 a=3.4445,b=−4.7750,c=2.0315 The function ϕ(σ)\phi(\sigma)ϕ(σ) rapidly drives all σ∈(0,1]\sigma \in (0, 1]σ∈(0,1] toward the fixed point σ∗=1\sigma^* = 1σ∗=1 in typically 555 iterations: O=NewtonSchulz(X0,k=5)≈UV⊤ O = \text{NewtonSchulz}(X_0, k=5) \approx U V^\top O=NewtonSchulz(X0​,k=5)≈UV⊤

3. Complete Muon Update Algorithm

Muon integrates standard Nesterov momentum and adjusts for rectangular matrix geometries:

  1. Momentum accumulation: Mt=βMt−1+(1−β)Gt M_t = \beta M_{t-1} + (1 - \beta) G_t Mt​=βMt−1​+(1−β)Gt​
  2. Nesterov blend: M~t=(1−β)Gt+βMt \widetilde{M}_t = (1 - \beta) G_t + \beta M_t Mt​=(1−β)Gt​+βMt​
  3. Newton–Schulz orthogonalization: Ot=NewtonSchulz(M~t) O_t = \text{NewtonSchulz}(\widetilde{M}_t) Ot​=NewtonSchulz(Mt​)
  4. Aspect ratio scaling: For an n×mn \times mn×m matrix, an orthogonal matrix has entries scaling as O(1/max⁡(n,m))O(1/\sqrt{\max(n, m)})O(1/max(n,m)​). To maintain uniform Root-Mean-Square (RMS) parameter update magnitudes across arbitrary layer dimensions, the update is scaled by: γ=max⁡(1,nm) \gamma = \sqrt{\max\left(1, \frac{n}{m}\right)} γ=max(1,mn​)​
  5. Weight update with decoupled decay: Wt+1=Wt−ηt(γOt+λWt) W_{t+1} = W_t - \eta_t \left( \gamma O_t + \lambda W_t \right) Wt+1​=Wt​−ηt​(γOt​+λWt​)

Comparison: Why Muon Differs from Adam and SGD

Feature SGD Adam / AdamW Muon
Geometry Euclidean (ℓ2\ell_2ℓ2​) norm Coordinate-wise (ℓ∞\ell_\inftyℓ∞​) norm Matrix Operator (Spectral / Schatten-∞\infty∞)
Effective Update GGG sign⁡(G)\operatorname{sign}(G)sign(G) (entrywise) UV⊤UV^\topUV⊤ (orthogonal polar factor)
Singular Value Handling Propagates Σ\SigmaΣ directly Distorts directions entrywise Equalizes all non-zero σi→1\sigma_i\to 1σi​→1
Optimizer States 1 buffer (MMM) 2 buffers (M,VM,VM,V) 1 buffer (MMM)
Application Domain General All layers (embeddings, biases, 1D) Exclusively 2D hidden linear/attention matrices

item.title: NorMuon
item.description:
NorMuon (Neuron-wise Normalized Muon) is an optimizer designed to address an imbalance in standard Muon: while Muon’s matrix orthogonalization improves the overall condition number of weight updates, individual neuron update norms vary dramatically across rows.

ResearchGate

NorMuon combines Muon’s polar/spectral orthogonalization with neuron-level (row-wise) adaptive scaling inspired by Adam and Adam-mini.

arXiv

1. The Motivation: Muon’s “Neuron-Imbalance” Problem

In neural network linear layers (W∈Rm×nW \in \mathbb{R}^{m \times n}W∈Rm×n where mmm is the output dimension/neuron count and nnn is input dimension), each row Wi,:W_{i,:}Wi,:​ represents the incoming connection weights for a single neuron.

ResearchGate

  • Muon’s strength: It projects the momentum matrix MMM to an approximately orthogonal matrix O≈UV⊤O \approx UV^\topO≈UV⊤ via Newton–Schulz iterations. This eliminates ill-conditioned singular values, equalizing step sizes along spectral principal directions. ResearchGate+ 1
  • Muon’s hidden flaw: Although the singular values of OOO are all approximately 111, the Euclidean norm of individual rows ∥Oi,:∥2\Vert{}O_{i,:}\Vert{}_2∥Oi,:​∥2​ (the per-neuron update magnitude) exhibits high variance. Some neurons receive disproportionately aggressive updates while others barely move, causing uneven feature utilization. ResearchGate
  • AdamW’s behavior: AdamW applies coordinate-level second-moment scaling (1/v+ϵ1 / \sqrt{v + \epsilon}1/v+ϵ​), which inadvertently regularizes per-neuron norms to be uniform, but fails to fix whole-matrix conditioning. ResearchGate+ 1

NorMuon proves that matrix-level orthogonalization and neuron-level adaptive normalization are complementary rather than conflicting.

ResearchGate

2. Mathematical Formulation

Let the parameter matrix be Wt∈Rm×nW_t \in \mathbb{R}^{m \times n}Wt​∈Rm×n and the objective gradient be Gt=∇WL(Wt)G_t = \nabla_W \mathcal{L}(W_t)Gt​=∇W​L(Wt​).

Step 1: First-Order Momentum Accumulation

Mt=β1Mt−1+(1−β1)Gt M_t = \beta_1 M_{t-1} + (1 - \beta_1) G_t Mt​=β1​Mt−1​+(1−β1​)Gt​

Step 2: Newton–Schulz Orthogonalization (Muon Step)

The momentum matrix is orthogonalized using quintic Newton–Schulz iterations (NS5\text{NS}_5NS5​) starting from Frobenius-normalized momentum X0=Mt/(∥Mt∥F+ϵ)X_0 = M_t / (\Vert{}M_t\Vert{}_F + \epsilon)X0​=Mt​/(∥Mt​∥F​+ϵ):

ResearchGate

Ot=NS5(Mt)≈UV⊤ O_t = \text{NS}_5(M_t) \approx U V^\top Ot​=NS5​(Mt​)≈UV⊤

Step 3: Neuron-wise Second Moment Tracking

ResearchGate

Instead of tracking a full m×nm \times nm×n second-moment tensor like Adam (which is memory-heavy), NorMuon tracks a 1D vector vt∈Rmv_t \in \mathbb{R}^mvt​∈Rm representing the average squared energy per row of the orthogonalized update OtO_tOt​:

ResearchGate

vt=β2vt−1+(1−β2)⋅mean⁡cols(Ot⊙Ot) v_t = \beta_2 v_{t-1} + (1 - \beta_2) \cdot \operatorname{mean}_{\text{cols}}(O_t \odot O_t) vt​=β2​vt−1​+(1−β2​)⋅meancols​(Ot​⊙Ot​)

where ⊙\odot⊙ denotes element-wise multiplication, and mean⁡cols\operatorname{mean}_{\text{cols}}meancols​ computes the mean along row dimension:

(vt)i=β2(vt−1)i+(1−β2)1n∑j=1n(Ot)ij2 (v_t)_i = \beta_2 (v_{t-1})_i + (1 - \beta_2) \frac{1}{n} \sum_{j=1}^n (O_t)_{ij}^2 (vt​)i​=β2​(vt−1​)i​+(1−β2​)n1​j=1∑n​(Ot​)ij2​

Step 4: Row-Wise Adaptive Normalization

The vector vt∈Rmv_t \in \mathbb{R}^mvt​∈Rm is broadcast across columns to create Vt∈Rm×nV_t \in \mathbb{R}^{m \times n}Vt​∈Rm×n (Vij=(vt)iV_{ij} = (v_t)_iVij​=(vt​)i​). The orthogonalized update is scaled entrywise by the inverse root of the neuron energy:

O^t=Ot⊘(Vt+ϵ) \widehat{O}_t = O_t \oslash \left( \sqrt{V_t} + \epsilon \right) Ot​=Ot​⊘(Vt​​+ϵ)

This guarantees that all neuron rows update at equalized relative speeds.

Step 5: Global Calibration and Weight Update

To prevent the scaling from drifting the effective global step size across different layer shapes, the update matrix is re-calibrated using the theoretical Frobenius expectation mn\sqrt{mn}mn​ and a standard scaling coefficient (typically 0.20.20.2):

η^t=0.2⋅ηt⋅mn∥O^t∥F \widehat{\eta}_t = 0.2 \cdot \eta_t \cdot \frac{\sqrt{mn}}{\Vert{}\widehat{O}_t\Vert{}_F} η​t​=0.2⋅ηt​⋅∥Ot​∥F​mn​​Wt+1=Wt−ηtλWt−η^tO^t W_{t+1} = W_t - \eta_t \lambda W_t - \widehat{\eta}_t \widehat{O}_t Wt+1​=Wt​−ηt​λWt​−η​t​Ot​

(where λ\lambdaλ is decoupled weight decay and ηt\eta_tηt​ is the base learning rate).

3. Comparison Across Optimizers

Property AdamW Standard Muon NorMuon
Geometry Coordinate-wise (ℓ∞\ell_\inftyℓ∞​) Spectral (S∞S_\inftyS∞​) Spectral + Neuron-wise ℓ2\ell_2ℓ2​
Matrix Condition Number Poor to Moderate Well-conditioned (≈1\approx 1≈1) Well-conditioned (≈1\approx 1≈1)
Per-Neuron Update Variance Low (Uniform) High (Imbalanced) Low (Uniform)
Optimizer Memory 2×2\times2× param count (M,VM,VM,V) 1×1\times1× param count (MMM) 1×1\times1× param count +O(m)+O(m)+O(m) per matrix
Distributed Communication Fully local row/col ops Requires all-gather for SVD/NS5 All-gather for NS5; local row normalization in FSDP2

4. Why Distributed Scaling (FSDP2) Works Well

ResearchGate

Under modern Fully Sharded Data Parallelism (FSDP2), parameters are partitioned row-wise across GPUs:

ResearchGate+ 1

  • The orthogonalization step (NS5\text{NS}_5NS5​) requires matrix multiplications across the full matrix, which is assigned round-robin across GPUs. arXiv
  • The row-normalization step is purely local: because FSDP2 shards parameter matrices by whole rows, each rank calculates the row-wise second moment vtv_tvt​ on its own local shard without any cross-device communication overhead

item.title: Ideal optimizer
item.description:
An ideal optimizer must balance convergence rate, generalization performance, numerical stability, memory footprint, and compute overhead. In high-dimensional deep learning and LLM training, optimization is dominated by ill-conditioned curvature, stochastic gradient noise, and GPU hardware constraints.

The core characteristics that define an ideal optimizer include:

1. Curvature Invariance (Handling Ill-Conditioned Surfaces)

  • The Problem: Loss landscapes are heavily ill-conditioned ravines where the condition number of the Hessian κ=λmax⁡λmin⁡\kappa = \frac{\lambda_{\max}}{\lambda_{\min}}κ=λmin​λmax​​ is massive (10410^4104 to 10810^8108). Standard gradient descent oscillates violently along directions of high curvature while making near-zero progress along flat directions.
  • The Ideal Behavior: The optimizer should adapt its effective step size per coordinate or per subspace according to the local curvature.
    • In second-order methods, pre-multiplying by H−1H^{-1}H−1 reshapes the anisotropic valley into an isotropic sphere.
      • In adaptive first-order methods (AdamW, RMSprop), dividing by vt\sqrt{v_t}vt​​ acts as a diagonal pre-conditioner approximating the inverse diagonal Hessian: θt+1=θt−η diag(H)−1/2gt \theta_{t+1} = \theta_t - \eta \, \text{diag}(H)^{-1/2} g_t θt+1​=θt​−ηdiag(H)−1/2gt​
  • Modern Invariance: Recent optimizers (like Muon) go further by enforcing spectral norm invariance via orthogonal updates, ensuring update steps do not privilege dominant singular vectors.

2. Fast Convergence and High Sample Efficiency

  • Escape from Saddles and Plateaus: Deep networks contain exponentially more saddle points than local minima. An ideal optimizer must maintain non-zero velocity through flat regions (gt≈0g_t \approx 0gt​≈0) via momentum (mtm_tmt​).
  • Lookahead and Damping: It should incorporate predictive momentum (such as Nesterov acceleration) to damp oscillations when approaching a minimum, preventing overshooting and allowing higher learning rates early in training.

3. Generalization to Unseen Data (Flat vs. Sharp Minima)

  • The Sharpness Problem: An optimizer that converges rapidly to the nearest empirical minimum often lands in a sharp minimum—a steep valley where small shifts between the training set and validation set distribution cause drastic increases in loss.
  • The Ideal Behavior: The optimizer should actively seek flat minima with wide basins, which generalize significantly better.
    • SGD with moderate batch sizes naturally discovers flat minima due to stochastic isotropic noise: Cov(Δθ)∝ηBΣ \text{Cov}(\Delta \theta) \propto \frac{\eta}{B} \Sigma Cov(Δθ)∝Bη​Σ
      • Modern loss-aware optimizers (e.g., Sharpness-Aware Minimization / SAM) explicitly optimize for flatness: min⁡θmax⁡∥ϵ∥≤ρL(θ+ϵ) \min_\theta \max_{\Vert{}\epsilon\Vert{} \le \rho} L(\theta + \epsilon) θmin​∥ϵ∥≤ρmax​L(θ+ϵ)

4. Minimal Memory Footprint (Optimizer State Overhead)

  • In large-scale training, model parameters are rarely the primary memory bottleneck; the optimizer states are:
    • FP32 Master Weights: 4 bytes / parameter4 \text{ bytes / parameter}4 bytes / parameter
      • AdamW (mt+vtm_t + v_tmt​+vt​): 4+4=8 bytes / parameter4 + 4 = 8 \text{ bytes / parameter}4+4=8 bytes / parameter
      • For a 70B parameter model, AdamW alone requires ∼560 GB\sim 560\text{ GB}∼560 GB of VRAM just to store state tensors.
  • The Ideal Metric: The optimizer should achieve adaptive, second-order-like behavior while approaching 000 to 444 bytes per parameter in auxiliary memory:
    • Discarding the second moment entirely (Lion: 4 bytes4\text{ bytes}4 bytes).
      • Factorizing 2D states into low-rank representations (Adafactor: O(R+C)O(R + C)O(R+C) instead of O(RC)O(RC)O(RC)).
      • Block-wise non-linear 8-bit dynamic quantization (8-bit Adam: 2 bytes2\text{ bytes}2 bytes).

5. Scale & Reparameterization Invariance

  • Layer-Wise Scale Disparities: Gradients in early transformer layers often differ in magnitude by multiple orders of magnitude compared to final projection heads.
  • The Ideal Behavior: The update step should be invariant to affine re-scalings of the loss, the weights, or the activations:
    • If weights WWW are scaled by a constant ccc, the effective trajectory should remain unchanged.
      • Optimizers like LARS and LAMB achieve this by scaling updates using layer-wise trust ratios: Δθ(l)∝∥θ(l)∥∥r(l)∥ \Delta \theta^{(l)} \propto \frac{\Vert{}\theta^{(l)}\Vert{}}{\Vert{}r^{(l)}\Vert{}} Δθ(l)∝∥r(l)∥∥θ(l)∥​
      • Lion enforces scale invariance at the coordinate level using the sign operator: Δθ∈{−η,+η}d\Delta \theta \in \{-\eta, +\eta\}^dΔθ∈{−η,+η}d.

6. Robustness to Hyperparameter Variations

  • Hyperparameter Sensitivity: Real-world training at scale cannot afford grid searches over learning rates, warmups, and decays due to multi-million-dollar compute budgets.
  • The Ideal Behavior:
    • Wide stability plateaus for learning rate η\etaη.
      • Minimal reliance on hand-crafted warmups or ad-hoc learning rate decay schedules (e.g., cosine, WSD).
      • Insensitivity to the batch size BBB, smoothly scaling from small single-GPU batches to massive distributed clusters without divergence.

7. Decoupled Regularization Mechanics

  • Proper Weight Decay: An optimizer must separate parameter updates derived from gradient error signals from regularizing decay.
  • The Flaw in Classical Optimizers: Coupling weight decay into the gradient gt+λθtg_t + \lambda \theta_tgt​+λθt​ within adaptive optimizers (as in standard Adam with L2L_2L2​) causes heavily updated parameters to receive less weight decay than rarely updated ones.
  • The Requirement: Decoupled weight decay (the AdamW formulation): θt+1=θt(1−ηλ)−η⋅Update(gt) \theta_{t+1} = \theta_t (1 - \eta \lambda) - \eta \cdot \text{Update}(g_t) θt+1​=θt​(1−ηλ)−η⋅Update(gt​) This guarantees a uniform rate of decay per step independent of gradient magnitude history.

8. Hardware & Kernel Friendliness

  • Compute vs. Memory Bandwidth: In modern GPU/TPU architectures, optimizer steps are bounded by memory bandwidth (HBM I/O), not arithmetic FLOPs.
  • The Ideal Optimizer:
    • Avoids frequent non-local tensor communications or global reductions.
      • Can be implemented as a single fused kernel (combining parameter load, gradient load, state update, weight decay, and store in one sweep through GPU SRAM).
      • Minimizes transcendental function evaluations or uncoalesced memory reads across distributed ranks.

Evaluation of Common Optimizers Against Ideal Criteria

Criterion SGD + Momentum AdamW Lion Muon Ideal Target
Curvature Adaptation Poor High (Diagonal) Moderate High (Spectral) Full / Block Curvature
Generalization (Flatness) Excellent Moderate Good Excellent Maximum
Optimizer Memory 4 B/param 8 B/param 4 B/param 4 B/param ≤4\le 4≤4 B/param
Scale Invariance Low High Very High High Exact
Batch Size Scalability Low (diverges large) Moderate High High Fully Invariant
Kernel Fusion Ease High High Highest (sign) Moderate (SVD/Newton) High
